vignette:
The Weight of What He Carried Home

Marcus is twenty-eight years old and works from a small home office in the flat he shares with his girlfriend, Lena, in a mid-sized city in the Netherlands. On most mornings, he sits in front of two monitors, scheduling posts, drafting copy, and monitoring engagement metrics for a portfolio of lifestyle brands. The work is quiet and predictable, which is exactly why he chose it. He needed something that would not ask too much of him — or so he thought.

Marcus served two tours with the Dutch Army, the second of which took him to Mali as part of a stabilization mission. He was twenty-four when a convoy he was part of struck an improvised explosive device on a dusty road outside a small village. The vehicle directly ahead of him was destroyed. He pulled two men from the wreckage. One survived. He held the other one — a twenty-two-year-old from Rotterdam named Daan — while he died. The whole sequence lasted perhaps eleven minutes. Marcus remembers every second of it with a clarity that still frightens him.

He left the military fourteen months after the incident, telling himself he simply wanted a different life. He moved in with Lena, who had waited for him, and enrolled in a digital marketing course. For a while, the busyness of building something new kept the worst of it at arm's length. But the distance was an illusion.

Now, nearly four years after Mali, Marcus rarely sleeps past three in the morning. He wakes with his heart pounding, sheets damp, the smell of smoke so vivid he sometimes checks the hallway before he remembers where he is. He does not always remember the dream itself, only the feeling it leaves behind — a cold, animal certainty that something terrible is about to happen. He lies still in the dark beside Lena, careful not to wake her, and waits for morning with the patience of someone who has learned that waiting is all he can do.

During the day, the intrusions come without warning. A car backfiring on the street below his office window can send him to the floor before he has consciously registered the sound. A news clip showing desert terrain, a particular quality of afternoon light, the smell of diesel — any of these can pull him back to that road in an instant, so completely that Lena sometimes has to say his name two or three times before he returns. He finds these moments humiliating in a way he cannot fully articulate, and he has stopped trying to explain them to her.

He avoids the news almost entirely now, which complicates his work in ways he manages through workarounds and scheduling tools. He has quietly dropped two clients whose content touched on conflict or geopolitics. His colleagues assume he is simply selective about the brands he takes on. He lets them think that.

What troubles Marcus most is not the fear, which he can sometimes manage, but the numbness that has settled over everything else. He loves Lena — he knows this in an abstract, factual way — but he struggles to feel it the way he once did. He goes through the motions of their life together: dinners, weekend walks, evenings on the sofa. He is present in body and largely absent in some other, harder-to-name way. Lena has begun asking questions he does not know how to answer. He tells her he is tired. This is true, but it is not the whole truth.

He has not spoken to anyone from his unit since leaving the service. He has Daan's mother's phone number saved in his contacts under a name he never calls. He has opened the contact screen perhaps a dozen times. He has never pressed dial. He is not sure what he would say to her, or what he is afraid she might say to him.
